name: Greedy Algorithms
analogy: Think of it as packing a small bag for a trip by always adding whichever remaining item is most useful right now, and never unpacking anything. It is fast and usually good, but it can miss a combination that only works if you skip the obvious first pick.

steps.title: Define the ranking rule
steps.description: Decide how to judge the next best choice. The whole quality of a greedy method depends on this rule, so it is the one design decision that matters.
steps.inExample: The rule is the gain in validation score that a candidate feature adds on top of the features already chosen.

steps.title: Start from nothing
steps.description: Begin with an empty selection and a fixed limit on how many items to pick, or a stopping rule.
steps.inExample: No features chosen yet; up to 3 may be picked from 6 candidates; the baseline score is 50 percent, meaning no ranking skill.

steps.title: Try each remaining item once
steps.description: For every item not yet chosen, work out what adding it would gain. This is done one round at a time with only the current selection in place.
steps.inExample: In round one, each of 6 features is tested alone and the relative strength index lifts the score to 53 percent, the best of the six.

steps.title: Lock in the best item
steps.description: Add the item with the biggest gain and never reconsider it. This is what makes the method fast, and also what makes it blind to combinations.
steps.inExample: The relative strength index is locked in and cannot be removed later, even if two other features would have worked better as a pair.

steps.title: Repeat with the updated selection
steps.description: Gains are re-measured given what is already chosen, so an item that overlaps with a chosen one now looks less useful.
steps.inExample: In round two the volume ratio lifts the score to 54 percent, while a feature similar to the relative strength index adds almost nothing.

steps.title: Stop at the limit or when gains vanish
steps.description: Stop when the limit is reached or when the best remaining gain is too small to matter. The chosen list is the answer.
steps.inExample: Round three adds the average true range for a score of 55 percent, and the limit of 3 features is reached.

useFor.example: Adding features one at a time to an MNQ direction model, keeping each only if it lifts the validation score.
Filling a margin budget by repeatedly taking the setup with the best expected score per margin dollar when the decision must be made in milliseconds.
Sending each slice of a parent order to the venue with the lowest marginal cost at that moment.

useFor.task: Building a starting solution for a search
useFor.example: Producing a quick first candidate that a metaheuristic or exact solver then improves.

avoidWhen: Items only work as a pair and are useless alone; greedy picks one at a time, misses the pair, and an exact or evolutionary search is better.
You need a proof of the best answer; use branch and bound, since greedy gives no guarantee unless the problem has a special structure.

example.scenario: A researcher wants the best three of six candidate features for an MNQ 5-minute direction model and adds them one at a time, always taking the one that lifts the validation score most.

input.summary: Six candidate features, a limit of three, and a way to score any chosen set.

fields.name: candidate features
fields.meaning: Relative strength index, volume ratio, average true range, 50-bar distance, 6-bar return and time of day.

fields.name: baseline score
fields.meaning: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve with no features; 50 percent means no skill.

fields.name: scoring method
fields.meaning: Each set is scored on walk-forward folds that were not used to fit it.

fields.name: minimum useful gain
fields.meaning: Selection stops when no remaining feature adds at least this much.

output.summary: The chosen features in order and the score after each addition.

fields.name: first choice
fields.meaning: Best single feature, a gain of 3 points.

fields.name: final score
fields.meaning: Validation score of the three-feature set.

example.reading: The gains of 3, 1 and 1 points show diminishing returns. Greedy does not guarantee the best three; a pair that works only together may have been missed. The set was picked because it scored well on these folds, so check it against a random-subset baseline on later folds.
